title: Climate, Pandemics and the Shape of the Future

cards.h: Two things changed everyday life in a way no army did
cards.b:
In March 2020, much of the world locked down within weeks because of a virus. And the same decade is on track to be the hottest in recorded history.

This last lesson is about the stories still being written.

Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air. Earth has warmed by about 1.1-1.3 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s, according to major scientific bodies. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees, aiming for 1.5.

More heat waves, heavier rains, melting glaciers and rising seas. Poorer countries, which emitted least, often suffer most. Climate talks keep arguing over who should cut emissions and who should pay: this is the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities'.

The first cases were found in Wuhan in late 2019. The WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Vaccines using new mRNA technology arrived in under a year. The WHO estimated about 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-21, far higher than the 7 million officially reported.

Pandemics are not new: the 1918 flu killed tens of millions.

Artificial intelligence advanced quickly after 2022. Debates continue about jobs, deepfakes and control. Meanwhile, wars, trade rivalries and shifting power shape the global order.

Nobody knows how it ends. History does not predict, but it gives you better questions.

cards.h: Do scientists disagree about climate change?
cards.b:
Myth: scientists are split.Fact: studies find overwhelming agreement among climate scientists that humans are warming the planet. The real arguments are about speed, local effects and the best policies.

Similarly, 'pandemics are one-offs' is wrong: experts expect more, which is why surveillance matters.

Solar, monsoon and vaccines

India links climate and health to its own fate. The monsoon feeds its farms, but heatwaves and floods have grown worse. At COP26 in Glasgow in November 2021, India promised net zero emissions by 2070.

In November 2015 Narendra Modi and France's François Hollande launched the International Solar Alliance in Paris. Its headquarters is in Gurugram, and it aims to bring cheap solar power to sunny countries.

In the pandemic, the Serum Institute of India in Pune made Covishield, the AstraZeneca vaccine, under licence. From January 2021 India's Vaccine Maitri programme sent doses to dozens of countries, though a deadly second wave in April and May 2021 forced exports to pause.

Five things to remember

  1. Human emissions are warming Earth.
  2. Paris (2015) set the 1.5-2 degree goals.
  3. COVID-19 was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020.
  4. Climate and health are global, shared problems.
  5. India pledged net zero by 2070.

Think about it

  • Who should pay for climate action?
  • Which lesson from history helps most with the future?
